notes.3: A very large majority of candidates understood the significance of the gradient of a speed-time graph.
notes.4: In this question on comparing masses and weights, 24% believed that balanced scales could indicate the same weight but different masses, revealing a misunderstanding of the relationship between mass and weight.
notes.7: This question on stability was well answered, with the most common incorrect answer being B (the cuboid), where candidates have not appreciated that A has the lowest centre of mass.
notes.8: Only 40% of responses were correct here. Most candidates failed to appreciate that, because the parcel was moving at constant speed, the resultant force on it must be zero. Therefore, the two forces mentioned must be equal in size and opposite in direction.
notes.9: Almost a fifth of candidates believed that nuclear energy in a power station is first converted into chemical energy, rather than into thermal energy.
notes.11: The transfer of energy from gravitational potential into other forms was very well understood.
notes.12: This concerned simple recall of the use of a mercury barometer, and rather surprisingly, just over half of the responses were incorrect.
notes.13: Most candidates believed that the water pressure on the larger section of the dam would be greater than that on the smaller section, ignoring the fact that the depth of the water was the same everywhere.
notes.15: Little difficulty was experienced with this question on melting and boiling points.
notes.18: A significant number of candidates opted for distractor A (smallest temperature rise), showing confusion over the concept of thermal capacity.
notes.23: Just over half the candidates knew where to place an object relative to a converging lens in order to produce a diminished image.
notes.24: This question required knowledge that a ray of light travelling from water to a less dense medium (air) would be partially reflected, as well as being refracted. Most candidates did not know that some reflection would occur for angles of incidence below the critical angle.
notes.26: The most common error here was to link small frequency to high-pitched sounds.
notes.27: Just over half the candidates failed to identify iron and steel as ferrous, many believing steel to be non- ferrous.
notes.33: This question on the potential divider showed evidence of widespread guessing, suggesting that the concept and operation was not very securely understood.
notes.40: Very few candidates failed to recognise the neutron as the non-charged particle.
